storylines.title: They trailed in every game of the series. They won it anyway.
storylines.observation: The Milwaukee Brewers swept the two-time defending champion Dodgers in the NLCS for their first pennant since 1982, then beat Tampa Bay in five games for the first World Series title in franchise history - a 57-year wait that outlasted a blown 3-0 lead.
storylines.question: What does it mean to win every game of a series without ever actually being ahead until the moment that mattered?
storylines.hidden_question: Does a result like this reveal something real about a team's character, or is it just the kind of statistical oddity that looks meaningful only in hindsight?
storylines.pattern: a decisive, clean-looking outcome built out of narrow, late comebacks rather than sustained dominance
storylines.why_now: Dormant: the arc this card tracks - the comeback pattern through the title and the parade - is complete. The offseason has begun (free agency, trade rumors), but that's a different story than the one this card is telling; holding until a genuinely new angle on the championship itself surfaces.
storylines.season_or_time_context: World Series Game 1 played Oct 23, 2026; Game 2 Oct 24

history.note: Milwaukee held its championship parade Friday, Oct 30: down Wisconsin Avenue at 10 a.m., ending at Henry Maier Festival Park for a free rally. The same city gave the 1982 team a parade after a Game 7 loss - this time there was a title to go with it.

Game 5: Brewers 4, Rays 1. Milwaukee closed out the series 4-1 at Tropicana Field for its first World Series title ever. William Contreras was named Series MVP; Trevor Megill recorded a 6-out save to finish it.

Game 4: Rays 4, Brewers 3 (12 innings). Cooper Pratt's homer put Milwaukee ahead in the top of the 12th; Tampa Bay answered with two in the bottom, Ben Williamson's hit walking it off. Series now 3-1; Milwaukee can still clinch in Game 5.

Game 3: Brewers 10, Rays 1. An eight-run fifth inning - a World Series record, built on seven straight hits - ended any suspense; Milwaukee takes a 3-0 series lead and can clinch the title with a win in Game 4.

Game 2: Brewers 5, Rays 4. Tampa Bay scored four in the top of the first; Milwaukee tied it on Sal Frelick's sixth-inning homer, took the lead in the seventh on a Cooper Pratt RBI, and closed it out - a 2-0 series lead built from another come-from-behind win.

storylines.title: Two countries that made peace in 2018 are undoing it in real time
storylines.observation: Ethiopia and Eritrea severed diplomatic ties on October 1 after the Tigray People's Liberation Front launched a major offensive against federal forces, reviving a conflict both sides had declared over in 2022 and raising fears of a second border war between the two countries.
storylines.question: How much of a peace holds once the leaders who made it decide it no longer serves them?
storylines.hidden_question: Is the 2018-2022 Ethiopia-Eritrea rapprochement better understood as a genuine resolution, or as a pause that lasted exactly as long as both governments found it convenient?
storylines.pattern: a negotiated peace between old enemies unraveling once the domestic politics that made it convenient change
storylines.why_now: The TPLF's offensive collapsed: federal forces retook Mekelle and the rest of Tigray's strongholds, and on Oct 16 Addis Ababa installed a new interim administration - a mayor for Mekelle, a chief administrator, separate heads for security and economic recovery - with a six-month mandate to hold elections. The Western Tigray border dispute, and the Eritrea rupture itself, were both deferred rather than resolved.
storylines.season_or_time_context: Diplomatic ties severed Oct 1, 2026; fighting resumed late September; interim Tigray government installed Oct 16 with a 6-month election mandate

history.note: The TPLF lost Mekelle and its other strongholds; on Oct 16 Addis Ababa named an interim Tigray administration (a new mayor, chief administrator and security/economic recovery heads) with a 6-month mandate to organize elections. The Western Tigray dispute and the Eritrea rupture remain unresolved.

Ethiopia and Eritrea cut diplomatic ties Oct 1 after Eritrean soldiers were reported entering the Tigray towns of Adigrat and Idaga Hamus; the UN chief called for an immediate end to fighting across Tigray, Afar and Amhara on Oct 9-10, with no ceasefire talks announced since.

storylines.title: A high-school protest over classroom conditions became a nationwide movement about everything else
storylines.observation: What began in mid-September as a lyceens' protest over classroom conditions and the Parcoursup college-admissions platform has grown into weekly nationwide marches over the cost of living, drawing hundreds of thousands and clashes with police in multiple cities.
storylines.question: At what point does a protest about one specific grievance become a vessel for every other grievance a country is carrying?
storylines.hidden_question: Is the scale of a protest movement a measure of the original grievance, or of how much unrelated frustration it happened to be standing near?
storylines.pattern: a narrow, specific grievance absorbing a much larger, diffuse one until the original complaint becomes almost incidental
storylines.why_now: The Nov 5 general strike drew an Interior Ministry early-afternoon count of about 270,000 marchers in 180 demonstrations outside Paris, with black-bloc clashes in Lyon and incidents in Nantes; only about 81 of France's 3,700 lycees were confirmed blocked (student unions claimed over 1,000), and rail disruption was patchy rather than a full shutdown - a strike that widened the movement's base without necessarily widening its crowds.
storylines.season_or_time_context: Movement began mid-September 2026; weekly Saturday marches since, including Oct 17, Oct 24 and Oct 31; general strike held Nov 5

history.note: Nov 5 general strike: roughly 270,000 marched in 180 demonstrations outside Paris per an early-afternoon Interior Ministry count, with black-bloc clashes in Lyon and incidents in Nantes. Only 81 of 3,700 lycees were confirmed blocked (unions claimed 1,000+); rail disruption was patchy, not a full shutdown.

Ahead of Thursday's five-union general strike, SNCF rail unions confirmed they're joining (a day before the new TGV M's inaugural run) and private-school staff are walking out for the first time - the fight is shifting from weekend marches to a broader work stoppage.

Oct 31's final tally: 320,000 marched nationwide, down 22% from Oct 24 and 42% from Oct 17 - a third straight weekend of declining turnout, with 779 arrests and 116 officers injured. Mostly calm; a national strike is still set for Nov 5.

Organizers called for another Saturday march on Oct 31 (gilets jaunes floated their own 'acte III' the same day) plus an intersyndicale strike on Nov 5 - the movement is outlasting the lycees' own Toussaint break, which runs through Nov 2.

Oct 24: a second consecutive Saturday of nationwide marches over school conditions and living costs, with tens of thousands out in Paris, Toulouse, Lyon and Clermont-Ferrand and police using tear gas in two cities - a week after the Oct 17 march drew an official count of 550,000.

storylines.title: A president trailing in the polls just won anyway - and the loser won't accept it
storylines.observation: Lula da Silva won a fourth term as Brazil's president on October 25, narrowly defeating Flavio Bolsonaro, son of the former president, in the tightest runoff in the country's recent history, after trailing him in most pre-election polls.
storylines.question: What does it mean when the polls and the outcome disagree - does it say something about the polls, or about what happens once people actually vote?
storylines.hidden_question: Is a come-from-behind election win evidence that late deciders broke one way, or a sign that pre-election polling has become less reliable at measuring this kind of race?
storylines.pattern: a result that defies its own pre-vote polling, raising the question of what the polling missed rather than just who won
storylines.why_now: Dormant: the legal fight itself is ongoing (Flavio's abuse-of-power/cassacao filings, Lula's counter-filing against Flavio, both pending before the TSE), but three search passes since Monday turned up nothing dated past Oct 26 - no ruling, no new filing with a confirmed date. Holding until the TSE actually rules on something or a dated development lands.
storylines.season_or_time_context: Runoff held Oct 25, 2026; new term begins Jan 5, 2027

history.note: The TSE confirmed Lula's win. Flavio Bolsonaro announced election night he'd seek to annul the result, then dropped that bid by Monday - his campaign is pivoting to a narrower abuse-of-power claim instead, which allies reportedly see as a longer shot.

Lula won the Oct 25 runoff, 51.79% to 48.21%, despite trailing Flavio Bolsonaro in most pre-election polls and losing the first round to him outright. Bolsonaro says he will challenge the result in court rather than concede.

storylines.title: A new Fed chair's first contested vote
storylines.observation: The Federal Reserve held its benchmark rate at 3.75%-4% on October 28, Kevin Warsh's first contested decision as chair, with two policymakers dissenting in favor of a hike against a backdrop of inflation still running above target.
storylines.question: What does it mean for a new institution's leadership when its very first contested decision reveals the committee split rather than unified?
storylines.hidden_question: Is a split vote evidence of a healthily independent committee working through genuine uncertainty, or an early sign that this Fed chair hasn't yet built the consensus his predecessor had?
storylines.pattern: a new leader's early decisions get read for what they reveal about authority and consensus, not just the substance of the choice itself
storylines.why_now: Dormant: the next real decision point is the Dec 9 FOMC meeting, and nothing dated has surfaced since the Oct 28 decision despite a search for Warsh's post-meeting remarks - everything found was recycled August Jackson Hole coverage. Holding until a genuinely new, dated development (a speech, a leak, Dec 9 itself) lands.
storylines.season_or_time_context: FOMC meeting concluded Oct 28, 2026; next decision Dec 9, 2026

history.note: The Fed held rates at 3.75%-4% on Oct 28. Governors Cook and Hammack dissented in favor of a hike - up from a unanimous September vote - while new chair Kevin Warsh declined to signal his own view and pointed to December as the next decision point.

storylines.title: Halloween spending keeps hitting records, even as everything about it gets more expensive
storylines.observation: Americans are expected to spend a record $13.5 billion on Halloween this year - costumes, decorations and candy all individually topping $4 billion - even as candy prices have risen three times faster than inflation since 2021 and most shoppers blame tariffs.
storylines.question: Why does a holiday with no functional purpose, that costs more every year, keep getting more popular rather than less?
storylines.hidden_question: Is rising Halloween spending evidence that ritual spending is one of the last discretionary categories people protect even under inflation pressure, or just evidence that retailers have gotten better at making the holiday feel mandatory?
storylines.pattern: a discretionary ritual expense that keeps setting records even as its underlying costs rise faster than overall inflation - spending as a measure of what people refuse to cut
storylines.why_now: Dormant: Halloween has passed and the season's story is complete - a record year, now closed. Holding until next year's NRF survey or a genuinely new angle (post-season retail data, candy-industry followup) surfaces.
storylines.season_or_time_context: Halloween is Oct 31, 2026; NRF survey fielded Sept 1-9, 2026

history.note: NRF's annual survey projects a record $13.5 billion in US Halloween spending this year, with 74% of Americans planning to celebrate - even as candy prices have outpaced inflation threefold since 2021 and most shoppers expect tariffs to push costs higher still.

storylines.title: A 32-meter Catrina and a parade for the dead, scheduled to the minute
storylines.observation: Mexico City's Dia de Muertos season runs Oct 29-Nov 2, anchored by a 32-meter Catrina in the Zocalo and an Oct 31 parade of thousands along Paseo de la Reforma, with downtown building facades lit for the occasion - nearly all of it free.
storylines.question: What does it mean for a ritual of remembrance to be planned with the precision of a civic event - down to the exact height of the centerpiece and the exact route of the march?
storylines.hidden_question: Does scheduling grief this precisely make the ritual more meaningful by giving it shared structure, or does it turn mourning into spectacle once a city plans it like a parade route?
storylines.pattern: a ritual built around loss and remembrance staged with the same civic choreography as a parade or festival - logistics applied to grief
storylines.why_now: Dormant: the official season ended Nov 2 and the observance itself (Nov 1-2) has passed - a complete, closed arc for this year. Holding until next year's season or a genuinely new angle surfaces.
storylines.season_or_time_context: Dia de Muertos observed Nov 1-2; CDMX's official season runs Oct 29-Nov 2, 2026

history.note: Mexico City's Dia de Muertos season (Oct 29-Nov 2) centers on a 32-meter Catrina in the Zocalo and an Oct 31 parade of thousands down Paseo de la Reforma, part of roughly 5,000 events the city is running this season, almost all free to attend.

storylines.title: The country that gave up hosting a climate summit, then volunteered to run it anyway
storylines.observation: COP31 opens Nov 9 in Antalya, Turkey, but Australia - which withdrew its hosting bid in a deal with Turkey - will lead the actual negotiations as 'President of Negotiations,' while the UN's climate chief has already lowered expectations for the summit.
storylines.question: What does it mean to run the talks at a summit you turned down the chance to host?
storylines.hidden_question: Is splitting the hosting country from the negotiating leadership a sign of healthy burden-sharing in climate diplomacy, or evidence that nobody wanted full ownership of a summit expected to produce little?
storylines.pattern: an institution's ceremonial host and its substantive leader are different parties, which raises the question of who actually owns the outcome
storylines.why_now: Australia gave up its COP31 hosting bid in exchange for leading negotiations as 'President of Negotiations,' with a Pacific Pre-COP already held Oct 5-8 in Fiji and a leaders' event in Tuvalu; the summit itself runs Nov 9-20 in Antalya, and the UN's own climate chief has pre-emptively lowered expectations, saying not to expect 'big-ticket' negotiated outcomes this year.
storylines.season_or_time_context: Pacific Pre-COP held Oct 5-8, 2026; COP31 runs Nov 9-20, 2026 in Antalya

history.note: Australia gave up hosting COP31 in a deal that put Turkey in Antalya as host but Australia in charge of negotiations; the Pacific Pre-COP ran Oct 5-8 in Fiji and Tuvalu, and the main summit opens Nov 9 with expectations already lowered.

storylines.title: A loud election year, a quiet result: every incumbent on the ballot won
storylines.observation: In the first major vote since last year's wave election, New York's Kathy Hochul, Connecticut's Ned Lamont and New Jersey's Cory Booker all won reelection comfortably on Nov 3 - a status-quo night with none of 2025's drama.
storylines.question: What does it mean when an election cycle produces no upsets at all - is a quiet result evidence of stability, or just evidence that nobody was paying attention?
storylines.hidden_question: Is a status-quo election a sign of a healthy, settled electorate, or a sign that the real contest already happened in 2025 and this vote was never competitive to begin with?
storylines.pattern: an election with high pre-vote attention but a fully predictable outcome - the drama front-loaded into the buildup rather than the result
storylines.why_now: Hochul beat Blakeman roughly 60-40 in New York, Lamont won reelection in Connecticut, and Booker won back his New Jersey Senate seat - comfortable wins with no competitive statewide race in the region, a contrast with 2025's closely-fought Virginia and New Jersey governor races and the Mamdani upset in New York City.
storylines.season_or_time_context: Election held Nov 3, 2026; contrasts with Nov 2025's Virginia, New Jersey and NYC results

history.note: New York's Kathy Hochul (~60-40 over Blakeman), Connecticut's Ned Lamont and New Jersey's Cory Booker all won reelection comfortably on Nov 3 - a quiet, status-quo night, unlike 2025's competitive Virginia/New Jersey governor races and NYC's Mamdani upset.
